blocks.value: When one control statement, selection or repetition, is located within another, it is **nested**. An `if` can be nested inside another `if` or inside an `if...else`. A nested `if` allows a program to perform multiple selections.

Conditions are tested **top to bottom**, and the **first** one that is true wins: the rest are skipped entirely. That is why each condition only needs a lower bound: reaching `score >= 80` already proves the score is below 90.
**Order matters enormously here.** Reverse the chain and every passing score reports as `D`:

if (score >= 60)      { System.out.println("D"); }   // 95 matches this first
else if (score >= 70) { System.out.println("C"); }   // unreachable for any score
The inner `if` is only reached when the outer condition is already true, so "warm" means *at least 50 but under 110*. Nesting expresses "given that X, now decide Y."
Which if does an else belong to?
An `else` always belongs to the **nearest** `if` before it that does not already have one. Indentation does not change this, so a missing brace can attach the `else` to the wrong `if`:
Although the `else` is lined up with the outer `if`, Java pairs it with `if (b > 3)`. Braces make the intent explicit and fix it: `if (a > 3) { if (b > 3) { ... } } else { ... }`.
